title: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
summary: Lay data out around how hot loops read it. Count cache lines for AoS, SoA and blocked SoA, see why SIMD needs contiguous fields, and learn when each layout wins in ECS engines and columnar stores.
outcomes: Explain why a loop that reads one field of an array of structs wastes most of each cache line
Compute cache-line traffic for AoS vs SoA from record size and bytes touched
Explain why SIMD loops need contiguous fields and how blocked SoA (AoSoA) provides them
Choose AoS, SoA, AoSoA or a hot/cold split from a workload's access pattern
Describe how ECS chunks and columnar formats apply SoA in real systems

lessons.title: Why a loop over objects wastes most of each cache line

blocks.md: Picture a particle system with a million particles. The natural object-oriented design is one `struct Particle` holding everything about a particle, and one big array of them. That layout is called **array of structs (AoS)**: each record's fields sit next to each other, and records follow one after another.

blocks.caption: AoS: one array of whole records. The hot loop reads 4 of every 32 bytes.

blocks.md: Recall from the prerequisite course that the CPU never fetches a single float. Every miss brings in a whole **cache line**, which is 64 bytes on mainstream x86 CPUs (Richard Fabian notes 64 bytes as the size most hardware has settled on; some ARM chips use 128). A 32-byte particle means each line holds exactly two particles.

blocks.prompt: The loop above reads only `y`. Out of each 64-byte line it pulls in, how many bytes does it actually use?
blocks.reveal: **8 bytes out of 64, or 12.5%.** The line holds two particles, and the loop uses one 4-byte `y` from each. The other 56 bytes (x, z, both velocities, mass, id) ride along for nothing: they cost memory bandwidth and they evict useful data from the cache.

scenes.caption: Top: a cache line from the AoS array. It holds particle 0 (slots 0 to 7) and particle 1 (slots 8 to 15), every field interleaved.
The loop reads only y: slots 1 and 9. Two useful floats, 14 wasted ones. The memory system paid for all 16.
Bottom: the same line if all y values live in their own array. Every slot is a y the loop needs: 16 particles per line instead of 2.
Same 64 bytes of traffic, 8 times as much useful data. That ratio, not the instruction count, is what usually limits a loop like this.

blocks.md:
The alternative layout is **struct of arrays (SoA)**: one array per field, so all the `x` values are contiguous, then all the `y` values, and so on. Element `i` is no longer one object in memory; it is the `i`-th slot of every array.

**Data-oriented design** is the broader idea behind this choice. Fabian defines it as designing software by developing transformations for well-formed data, where *well-formed* is guided by the target hardware and by the transforms that will run over the data. You choose the layout from how the hot loops access the data, not from how you would describe the objects.

blocks.caption: SoA: the same loop now walks one dense 4-byte-stride array.

blocks.title: Cache lines read for one pass over 1,000,000 particles

scenes.caption: Loop reads only y. AoS streams all 32 MB: 500 k lines. SoA streams the 4 MB y array: 62.5 k lines, 8 times fewer.
Loop updates position from velocity (reads x, y, z, vx, vy, vz: 24 of 32 bytes). SoA reads 6 arrays, 375 k lines. The gain shrinks to 1.33x.
Loop touches all 8 fields. Both layouts move the same 32 MB, 500 k lines. SoA has nothing left to skip.

blocks.md: SoA is not automatically faster. Its advantage is exactly the fraction of each record that a loop does *not* touch. A loop that uses every field gains nothing from the layout change, and some access patterns get worse (lesson 2).
Memory moves in cache lines. Lay out data so that the bytes a hot loop needs are packed together, and the bytes it skips live somewhere else.

blocks.question: A loop over 1,000,000 AoS particles (32 bytes each) reads only `mass`. You move `mass` into its own float array. Roughly how many cache lines does the pass read now, assuming 64-byte lines?
options: 62,500, because each line now holds 16 masses instead of 2
500,000, because the number of particles did not change
250,000, because each line now holds twice as many masses
1,000,000, because each mass is a separate access
blocks.explain: The mass array is 4 MB. 4,000,000 bytes / 64 bytes per line = 62,500 lines. In AoS each line carried 2 masses, so the pass cost 500,000 lines. Lines are the unit of traffic, not elements.

blocks.question: Which loop gains the least from converting this Particle array from AoS to SoA?
options: A collision broad phase that reads only x and z
A save-to-disk routine that writes every field of every particle
A renderer that reads only position (x, y, z)
A query counting particles with mass above a threshold
blocks.explain: Writing every field touches all 32 bytes of each record, so AoS already uses every byte of each line. The other loops touch 4 to 12 bytes of 32 and get 2.7x to 8x less traffic with SoA.

lessons.title: Counting cache lines: the traffic model and the padding bonus

blocks.md: Lesson 1 suggests a simple model you can do in your head. Assume a loop makes one sequential pass over $N$ records, the hardware moves whole lines of $L$ bytes, and arrays are packed with no gaps. Let $S$ be the record size and let $s_f$ be the size of field $f$.

blocks.caption: AoS pays for the whole record. SoA pays only for the fields the loop touches.

blocks.md: Write $k = \sum s_f$ for the bytes the loop actually touches per record. The ratio of traffic is then $S/k$. For the particle with $S = 32$ and a loop that reads only `y` ($k = 4$), that is $32/4 = 8$. Play with the record size and touched bytes below.

scenes.caption: Reading 4 bytes per record: SoA stays flat at 62.5 lines per 1,000 records while AoS grows with the record size. At S = 32 it is 500, 8 times more.
Reading 24 bytes (position and velocity): SoA rises to 375. The gap at S = 32 is now only 500 vs 375.

Reading 12 bytes (position only): SoA needs 187.5 lines vs 500. Simplified model: it ignores prefetching, alignment and lines shared at array ends. It is still the right first estimate for streaming loops.

blocks.md: SoA has a second, quieter benefit: it removes **padding**. A compiler aligns each field to its natural boundary and rounds the struct size up to its largest alignment, so a struct holding an 8-byte integer and a 1-byte flag takes 16 bytes, 7 of them filler. Zig's standard library `MultiArrayList` is a SoA container, and its doc comment names this directly: storing each field in its own list "allows for memory savings if the struct or union has padding".

blocks.title: struct { a: u64, b: u8 } per element, in bytes

scenes.caption: AoS: 8 bytes of a, 1 byte of b, then 7 bytes of tail padding so the next element's a starts on an 8-byte boundary. 16 bytes per element.
SoA: the a array is a dense run of 8-byte values and the b array is a dense run of bytes. Each element costs 8 + 1 = 9 bytes.
9 instead of 16 bytes is 43.75% less memory, before any question of which fields a loop touches. A loop that reads only b now streams 1 byte per element instead of 16.

blocks.md: Now the flip side. Suppose you look up **one** particle by index and use every field, as a physics query or a network snapshot of a single object would. In AoS the 32-byte record sits in one line (two at most if it straddles a boundary). In SoA the same record is scattered over 8 arrays, so you touch 8 different lines, each mostly full of other particles' data.

blocks.prompt: A hash map returns particle indices in random order, and the code reads all 8 fields of each one. How many cache lines per lookup for AoS and for SoA?
blocks.reveal: **AoS: 1 line** (the 32-byte record fits in one 64-byte line if records are aligned). **SoA: 8 lines**, one in each field array. Random whole-record access is the case where AoS wins, and the model above predicts it: with random access, each touched field costs a full line instead of $s_f$ bytes.

blocks.md: SoA has real costs beyond random access. Adding or removing an element writes to every field array, the code needs one pointer or slice per field, and an element can no longer be passed around as one object. The ISPC performance guide calls hand-written SoA access syntax "messy", which is why tools like ISPC's `soa<8>` and Zig's `MultiArrayList` exist.
Traffic ratio for a streaming loop is $S/k$: record size over bytes touched. For random access to whole records, the ratio flips against SoA by up to the number of fields.

blocks.question: A 64-byte AoS record has 16 four-byte fields. A loop streams 10 million records and reads 2 fields. What does the model predict for AoS vs SoA traffic?
options: Equal: both read 10 million records
AoS reads 640 MB, SoA reads 80 MB, an 8x difference
AoS reads 640 MB, SoA reads 320 MB, a 2x difference
SoA reads more because it opens 2 separate streams
blocks.explain: AoS: 10M x 64 B = 640 MB. SoA: 10M x 8 B (two 4-byte fields) = 80 MB. The ratio is S/k = 64/8 = 8. Two streams is no problem for a sequential scan; the touched bytes are all useful.

blocks.question: Which workload is the best fit for keeping AoS?
options: Summing one numeric field over every row
Finding all records whose flag byte is set
Fetching a random record by id and returning all of its fields
Running the same arithmetic on x, y and z of every point with SIMD
blocks.explain: Random access to whole records uses every byte of the one line AoS brings in, while SoA would touch one line per field. The other three stream a few fields over many records, which is exactly where SoA (or blocked SoA for SIMD) wins.

lessons.title: SIMD lanes: contiguous loads, gathers, and blocked SoA

blocks.md: Cache lines are half the story. The other half is **SIMD** (single instruction, multiple data): one instruction operates on a whole vector register. A 256-bit AVX register holds 8 floats, so one add can update 8 particles at once, but only if the 8 inputs can be loaded into the register cheaply.

The cheapest way is a **contiguous vector load**: 8 adjacent floats, one instruction. If the 8 values are scattered, the CPU needs a **gather**, which loads each lane from its own address. The ISPC performance guide (ISPC is Intel's compiler that runs many copies of one function, called program instances, across the SIMD lanes of a CPU) states the rule plainly: memory access is best when program instances access a contiguous region, because then "efficient vector load and store instructions can often be used rather than gathers and scatters". It adds that not all CPUs have a gather instruction, in which case the compiler issues one scalar load per lane.

blocks.title: 8 points {float x, y, z;}: 96 bytes, 4 bytes per cell

scenes.caption: The same 96 bytes in two layouts. Cell 16 starts at byte 64, the second cache line if the array starts on a line boundary.
AoS: the 8 x values sit at byte offsets 0, 12, 24, ..., 84, a stride of 12 bytes spread over 88 bytes and 2 cache lines. Filling one register needs a gather.
Blocked SoA: x0 to x7 are adjacent, bytes 0 to 31. One 32-byte vector load fills all 8 lanes.
The y values are the next 32 bytes and the z values the 32 after that. Three loads bring in x, y and z for 8 points.

blocks.md: The lower row is not plain SoA. It is **AoSoA** (array of structs of arrays, also called blocked SoA): records are grouped into blocks of 8, and *inside* a block each field is a short array. ISPC builds this into its type system. Writing `soa<8> Point pts[...]` gives the layout `struct { float x[8], y[8], z[8]; }` per block, while the code keeps AoS syntax: `pts[i].x`.

Why block at all instead of one long array per field? A block keeps all fields of a record within 96 bytes of each other, so fetching one whole point touches 2 lines at most instead of one line in each of 3 far-apart arrays. It also needs only one base pointer. Vector loads still work because each field run (8 floats, 32 bytes) is exactly one AVX register.

blocks.title: Where does pts[i].x live in soa<8> Point?
blocks.code:
BLOCK = 8                 # records per block
FIELD_BYTES = 4 * BLOCK   # one float[8] run = 32 B
BLOCK_BYTES = 3 * FIELD_BYTES  # x, y, z = 96 B

def offset(i, field):     # field: 0=x, 1=y, 2=z
    block = i // BLOCK
    lane = i % BLOCK
    return block * BLOCK_BYTES + field * FIELD_BYTES + lane * 4

print(offset(10, 0), offset(10, 1), offset(10, 2))
print(offset(13, 0))

scenes.caption: Constants for the soa<8> Point layout: 8 records per block, 32 bytes per field run, 96 bytes per block.
Element 10 is in block 10 // 8 = 1, lane 10 % 8 = 2. This matches the ISPC guide: pts[10].x is the third x value of the second block.
x of element 10: 1 x 96 + 0 x 32 + 2 x 4 = 104. y adds one field run (136), z adds two (168).
Element 13: block 1, lane 5, x at 96 + 20 = 116. Elements 8 to 15 share block 1, so lanes 0 to 7 of one vector load are exactly elements 8 to 15.

blocks.md: The ISPC user guide spells out the cost: in `soa<8> Point`, `pts[1].x` and `pts[1].y` are separated by 7 float values. A single element is no longer contiguous. AoSoA trades a little whole-record locality for vector-friendly loads.

Vectorizing the instructions does not fix the layout. Even if a compiler vectorizes an AoS loop, the x values are still 12 bytes apart, so each register still needs a gather and the loop still pays for every unused byte in each line.

blocks.question: You vectorize `sum += pts[i].x` over AoS `Point {float x, y, z;}` with 8-wide AVX. What does the ISPC guide say the compiler must do to load 8 x values?
options: A gather (or one scalar load per lane on CPUs without gather), because the x values are 12 bytes apart
One aligned 32-byte vector load
Nothing special: the cache line already holds all 8 x values
Convert the array to SoA automatically at compile time
blocks.explain: The x values sit at offsets 0, 12, ..., 84, not adjacent, so a single contiguous load cannot fill the register. The guide says such an access "accesses non-sequential memory locations", so a gather is required. They also span 2 cache lines, not 1.

blocks.question: In `soa<8> Point pts[...]` (float x, y, z), what is the byte offset of `pts[17].z` from the start of the array?
blocks.explain: Block 17 // 8 = 2, lane 17 % 8 = 1. Each block is 96 bytes and z is the third 32-byte run. Offset = 2 x 96 + 2 x 32 + 1 x 4 = 260. 212 is the AoS answer (17 x 12 + 8), 204 is where record 17 starts in AoS, and 68 is plain SoA (17 x 4).

lessons.title: Worked example: binary search over animation keyframes

blocks.md: Fabian's book gives a concrete case. An animation track stores keyframes, each a 4-byte time plus 12 bytes of value data: 16 bytes per keyframe. To sample the animation at time $t$, you binary search the times for the last key at or before $t$. Only the times matter during the search; the value is read once at the end.

With AoS, the search reads 16-byte records, so each 64-byte line holds 4 times and 48 bytes of values the search ignores. With SoA, the times live in their own array (16 per line) and the values in another. Take a track of 128 keys whose key $i$ has time $i$, and search for $t = 77$.

blocks.code:
def search(n, t):              # last key with time <= t (times[i] = i)
    lo, hi = 0, n
    probes = []
    while hi - lo > 1:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        probes.append(mid)
        if mid <= t: lo = mid
        else: hi = mid
    return lo, probes

key, probes = search(128, 77)       # probes: 64 96 80 72 76 78 77
aos_lines  = {p * 16 // 64 for p in probes}   # 16-byte records
soa_lines  = {p * 4 // 64 for p in probes}    # 4-byte times
print(len(aos_lines), len(soa_lines))         # 5 3
blocks.caption: The script behind every number in this lesson: 7 probes, 5 distinct AoS lines, 3 distinct SoA lines.

blocks.prompt: The search makes 7 probes. How many distinct cache lines does each layout touch? (AoS: 4 keys per line. SoA times: 16 keys per line.)
blocks.reveal: **AoS 5 lines, SoA 3 lines** (plus 1 line of the values array to read the result, so 4). The early probes jump far apart and miss in both layouts. The difference appears once the range shrinks: SoA lands in a line it already has after 3 probes, AoS only after 5.

blocks.title: Cache lines touched while searching for t = 77

scenes.caption: Each cell is one 64-byte line. Rows 1 to 4: the 32 lines of the AoS array (4 keys each). Row 5: the 8 lines of the SoA times array (16 times each). A number marks the probe that first touched the line.
Probe 1 reads key 64. AoS: key 64 lives at byte 1024, cache line 16. SoA: time 64 is at byte 256, line 4 of the times array. Both are new misses.
Probe 2 reads key 96. AoS line 24 and SoA line 6: two more new lines each.
Probe 3 reads key 80. AoS line 20, SoA line 5. Still a miss on both sides.
Probe 4 reads key 72. AoS needs line 18 (a 4th line). SoA line 4 already holds times 64 to 79, so this probe is free.
Probe 5 reads key 76. AoS line 19 is new (5th line). SoA: still line 4.
Probe 6 reads key 78, also in AoS line 19 (keys 76 to 79). Once the range shrinks below 4 keys, AoS stops missing too.
Probe 7 reads key 77 and the search ends on key 77. Totals: AoS touched 5 lines, SoA touched 3 lines of times, then needs 1 more line (bytes 924 to 935 of the values array) to read the value.

blocks.md: One search is a small sample, so the script runs every target from 0 to 127. AoS touches 5 to 6 lines, 5.03 on average. SoA touches 3.13 lines of times on average, plus 1.13 lines of values (16 of the 128 values, 12 bytes each, straddle a line boundary): 4.25 in total. That is a 16% saving per search, not 4x.

blocks.title: Per search vs whole track, 128 keys

scenes.caption: Average lines touched per search over all 128 targets: 5.03 for AoS vs 4.25 for SoA (times plus the value line). A modest gain.
Lines the search can ever touch: the whole AoS array is 32 lines (2 KiB); the SoA times array is 8 lines (512 bytes). Many searches over one track keep all 8 hot in L1.

blocks.md: The second scene is the real win. A game samples many tracks every frame. The searched data in SoA is a quarter of the size, so it stays resident in the cache across lookups, and the cache space it frees holds other tracks. Fabian makes the same point: for a 128-key stream the times take up 8 cache lines in total. (Fabian's counts per search, "up to 5" AoS steps and "at most three" SoA lines, differ slightly from ours because the exact search loop differs; the shape of the result is the same.)
Measure what the hot path *reads repeatedly*. Splitting the search key from its payload shrinks the working set the loop revisits, which often matters more than the miss count of a single call.

blocks.question: You double the track to 256 keys but keep the same layouts. How large is the SoA times array, in 64-byte lines?
options: 8 lines
32 lines
64 lines
16 lines
blocks.explain: 256 times x 4 bytes = 1,024 bytes = 16 lines. The AoS array would be 256 x 16 = 4,096 bytes = 64 lines, still 4 times larger, because each record is 4 times the size of a time.

blocks.question: A teammate measures one cold lookup and finds SoA only 16% faster, so they conclude the split is pointless. What is the strongest reply?
options: The measurement must be wrong; SoA is always 4x faster here
Per-lookup misses are similar, but the searched data is 4x smaller, so across many lookups it stays cached and the gap widens
SoA only helps with SIMD, and binary search is not vectorized
They should switch to a linked list of keyframes
blocks.explain: A single cold lookup misses in both layouts on its first few probes. The benefit of a 512-byte index over a 2 KiB one shows up when many lookups reuse the same lines, which is how an animation system runs.

lessons.title: Choosing a layout: hot/cold splits, ECS chunks and columnar data

blocks.md:
Pure AoS and pure SoA are two ends of a range. In practice you pick per data set, from its hottest access patterns:

- **SoA** when loops stream a few fields of many records.
- **AoS** when you use most of a record at once, or reach records at random.
- **AoSoA** when SIMD loops need contiguous field runs but you still want a record's fields close together.
- **Hot/cold splitting** when one record has a few fields used every frame and many used rarely.

Hot/cold splitting is the lightest-weight version of SoA. Keep the fields the per-frame loop reads in a small hot struct, and move the rest to a parallel array indexed the same way. As an illustration, take 10,000 monsters with 128-byte records where the update loop needs 16 bytes.

scenes.caption: Before: the loop drags all 128 bytes of each monster through the cache. 10,000 x 128 / 64 = 20,000 lines.
After splitting: 10,000 x 16 / 64 = 2,500 lines, 8 times fewer. The cold 112 bytes are read only by code that needs them.

blocks.md: Fabian's book pushes the idea further with **existential processing**: instead of a boolean like `is_hurt` checked in every record, keep a separate table holding only the hurt entities. A row's existence encodes the boolean. The book's example: a regeneration system that runs over the health table skips the dead and the unhurt for free, because they are simply not in it.

Game engines built on an **entity component system (ECS)** apply these ideas at scale. Unity's Entities package groups entities by **archetype**, the exact set of component types they have. All entities of an archetype live in 16 KiB **chunks**, and each chunk contains one array per component type plus an array of entity IDs. That is AoSoA with 16 KiB blocks.

blocks.title: Unity Entities: archetype, chunks, per-component arrays

scenes.caption: Every entity with exactly components A and B belongs to one archetype. Its entities are stored in chunks.
Inside each 16 KiB chunk: one tightly packed array per component, plus the entity IDs. Index k in every array is the same entity.
A system that needs only A finds the matching archetypes, then streams each chunk's A array. B values never enter the cache.

blocks.md: Keeping arrays tightly packed has a consequence for removal. Unity's docs say that when an entity leaves a chunk, "the last entity of the chunk is moved to fill the gap". That keeps iteration dense, but it means an entity's index inside a chunk is not stable.

blocks.title: Removing entity e1 from a chunk

scenes.caption: Six entities packed at indices 0 to 5. Index k of every array belongs to the same entity.
e1 is removed (destroyed, or moved to another archetype). Its slot in every array is now a hole.
The last entity, e5, moves into slot 1 in every array. The chunk is dense again with 5 entities, but e5 now lives at a different index.

blocks.md: Other systems make the same trade explicit. Bevy's ECS lets each component choose its storage: `Table`, the default, "provides fast and cache-friendly iteration, but slower addition and removal", while `SparseSet` "provides fast addition and removal of components, but slower iteration". Analytics databases are SoA too: Fabian notes that column-oriented databases win at aggregation "simply because irrelevant data is not loaded". Apache Arrow's in-memory columnar format stores each column in contiguous buffers and recommends 64-byte alignment and padding so a loop can use 512-bit (AVX-512) SIMD loads without edge checks.

A common misconception, called out by Fabian himself: data-oriented design is not only about cache misses or splitting hot and cold fields. It is about designing around the data and the transforms on it. Layout is the most visible tool, not the whole method.
List the hot loops, write down which fields each one touches and whether it streams or jumps, then pick the layout that packs those bytes together. Re-measure when the access pattern changes.

blocks.question: Your ECS component `Transform` is read by rendering every frame, but you also add and remove a `Stunned` marker component on thousands of entities per second. Using Bevy's storage options, which setup fits?
options: Both as SparseSet, since additions are frequent
Transform as Table (default) for fast iteration, Stunned as SparseSet for cheap add and remove
Both as Table, because Table is always faster
Transform as SparseSet, Stunned as Table
blocks.explain: Table storage gives cache-friendly iteration but costs more on add and remove; SparseSet is the reverse. Transform is iterated constantly and rarely added, Stunned churns constantly, so each gets the storage that matches its access pattern.

blocks.question: In a Unity chunk, your code saved "entity e5 is at index 5" before e1 was destroyed. What is true afterwards?
options: Index 5 still holds e5
Index 5 now holds e1
e5 has moved to index 1, because the last entity fills the gap
The chunk keeps a hole at index 1 until it is compacted later
blocks.explain: Unity keeps chunk arrays tightly packed by moving the last entity into the freed slot. Indices inside a chunk are therefore not stable identities; use entity IDs for that.

blocks.question: A loop checks `if (e.is_burning)` on 100,000 entities every frame, and about 1% are burning. Following existential processing, what change helps most?
options: Pack is_burning into a bit field inside the entity struct
Keep a separate table of burning entities and run the loop only over it
Sort entities so burning ones come first, but keep the flag check
Move is_burning to the start of the struct
blocks.explain: With a burning table, row existence is the boolean. The loop touches about 1,000 rows instead of streaming the cache lines of all 100,000 entities just to read a flag that is almost always false.
